label: type
title: type chooses the connector contract
lead: Three runnable local declarations. Change the type and the meaning of connection and extract changes with it.
description: Choose the connector that interprets a source declaration.
goalText: A connector family, then the contract for the two blocks below it.
cases: table is interpreted as a file name
the declaration runs against the canonical orders
the same outer declaration keeps its shape
the target now contains JSON objects
type values are trimmed and lower-cased
the resulting connector is the same
tour: The catalogue that owns the declaration.
Every source identifier maps to exactly one connector declaration.
Changing this name changes the reference, not the connector type.
Hydra normalizes it, then asks the connector registry to build that type.
The selected type gives these blocks their meaning.
A table means a file to CSV and a table or query to a database connector.
definition: type is the discriminator that tells Hydra which connector must interpret a source declaration.
It is not a file format hint applied after reading. Connector construction happens first; that connector owns the accepted connection settings and extraction behavior.
contains: Whitespace is trimmed and the value is lower-cased.
CSV and JSON are built in; database and optional connectors use the same slot.
thesisTitle: The type changes the contract
thesis: The outer YAML stays stable while the inner meaning changes. Choose type first, then fill the connection and extraction blocks that belong to that connector.
diagramTitle: Type selects the connector contract
diagramDesc: The csv type selects the CSV connector, which interprets connection and extract to read orders.csv.
diagramFoot: The same keys are not interpreted by a generic reader; the selected connector owns them.
diagramCaption: One word selects the code that reads the rest of the declaration.

label: extract
title: extract narrows what the connector reads
lead: Three complete source declarations. The connector stays local; the extraction request changes.
description: Declare the object, query or collection a source connector must read.
goalText: A target plus optional limits and batching, after the connector has been selected.
cases:
sources:
  input:
    type: csv
    connection: {base_path: data/canonical}
    extract:
      table: orders.csv
      batch_size: 10000
table names the file for this connector

sources:
  input:
    type: csv
    connection: {base_path: data/canonical}
    extract:
      table: orders.csv
      batch_size: 10
the connector may yield several batches
batching does not change the rows

sources:
  input:
    type: json
    connection: {}
    extract:
      table: data/canonical/products.json
      limit: 100
the JSON connector receives a file target
tour: The request passed to the source connector.
It sits inside one source declaration, below type and connection.
Files and tables use table, SQL can use query, and MongoDB can use collection.
Limits narrow a read when the selected connector supports that option.
The maximum batch requested from the connector.
The default is 10,000; batching changes delivery, not row meaning.
definition: extract is the read request handed to the selected source connector.
It does not identify the connector or describe credentials. Those belong to type and connection; extraction begins only after both are resolved.
contains: Use table, query, or collection according to the connector.
batch_size defaults to 10,000 and must be at least 10 in the current parser.
thesisTitle: Connection reaches; extract chooses
thesis: A connection can reach an entire system. extract makes one concrete request inside it: this file, table, query, or collection, delivered in these batches.
diagramTitle: Extract turns a connection into a read request
diagramDesc: A reachable system is narrowed to one target and delivered as batches of rows.
diagramFoot: The connector is already known; extract tells it what to fetch.
diagramCaption: Reachability comes first; selection comes second.

label: schema
title: schema records expectations, not transformations
lead: Three valid schema policies. They describe incoming fields without replacing cast or select.
description: Describe expected source fields and schema policies.
goalText: Field metadata and policies attached to the source declaration.
cases: the block does not cast the CSV rows

sources:
  input:
    type: csv
    extract: {table: data/canonical/orders.csv}
    schema:
      mode: auto
      drift_policy: warn
      sample_size: 100
sample size must be at least one

sources:
  input:
    type: json
    extract: {table: data/canonical/products.json}
    schema:
      mode: hybrid
      fields:
        - {name: product_id, type: string}
      validation_policy: best_effort
declared fields and inferred shape may coexist
the policy is accepted by the source model
rows still flow to transformations unchanged
tour: An optional block inside a source.
Omit it when the source needs no declared expectations.
Accepted modes are auto, manual, infer_strict, and hybrid.
Each field has a name and type, plus optional path, required, default, array handling, and description.
These values are validated and stored with the source definition.
definition: schema is optional metadata describing the shape a source is expected to expose.
It is not a transformation step. In the current executor the block is parsed and validated, but it does not cast, select, or reject runtime rows; use transformations for those effects.
contains: Names, types, nested paths, required/default metadata, and array handling.
Drift, validation, and sampling settings validated by the source model.
thesisTitle: Expected is not transformed
thesis: A schema tells readers what the source is meant to look like. Only transformation steps change the rows, so keep operational casts and selections in transformations.yaml.
diagramTitle: Schema expectations are separate from row transformations
diagramDesc: The schema describes connector output while transformations perform casts and selections later.
diagramFoot: Description and mutation are separate responsibilities.
diagramCaption: Schema explains the boundary; transformations alter what crosses it.

label: type
title: type chooses the writer
lead: Three correct CSV declarations. The discriminator selects who interprets connection and load.
description: Choose the connector that writes a destination.
goalText: The connector responsible for opening the target and loading final rows.
cases: the connection resolves the output directory
the parser trims and lower-cases the value
the identifier changes independently of type
tour: pipeline.to chooses one declaration from this mapping.
A local name for the target declaration.
The identifier is what pipeline.to stores; it is not the table name.
It is normalized before Hydra asks the connector registry for a writer.
The blocks interpreted by that writer.
Connection reaches the target system; load names the object and policy.
definition: Destination type tells Hydra which connector must write the final rows.
It does not select the destination identifier or loading mode. Those remain separate so one connector family can serve many targets and policies.
contains: The value is stripped and lower-cased.
The registry builds the matching destination connector.
That connector owns the meaning of connection and load.
thesisTitle: Reading and writing share a vocabulary
thesis: Sources and destinations use the same type slot, but the selected connector is built for a direction. Here it must accept final rows and apply the declared load policy.
diagramTitle: Destination type selects a writer
diagramDesc: The csv type selects the CSV destination connector that writes result.csv.
diagramFoot: The direction is destination: the connector receives rows rather than producing them.
diagramCaption: The discriminator chooses the writer; load chooses its target.

label: connection
title: connection reaches the target system
lead: Three valid CSV connections. Location stays separate from the file and write mode.
description: Configure how a destination connector reaches its target system.
goalText: The system or directory the selected writer can reach before loading begins.
cases:
destinations:
  output:
    type: csv
    connection:
      base_path: examples/tutorial/dsl-elements/out
    load: {table: result.csv, mode: replace}
the CSV writer resolves one base directory
an empty mapping is valid for CSV
the connector falls back to the job directory
load still names the target file
the target name and mode change in load
tour: The mapping is interpreted only after destination type selects a connector.
Other connector types use their own host, port, database, or authentication keys.
The object to write is not connection data.
Keeping it in load lets one connection serve several targets.
Reachability does not decide append or replace.
The write policy belongs to the target declaration in load.
definition: Destination connection is the mapping used to reach the system that will receive rows.
It does not name the table or decide append, replace, or upsert. Those are loading concerns and remain in load.
contains: CSV uses a base path; databases use network and database settings.
Secrets belong in placeholders and load behavior belongs elsewhere.
One reachable system can host several target objects.
thesisTitle: Reach the system before naming the object
thesis: Connection answers “where can this writer connect?” Load answers “what should it write there, and how?” Keeping those questions apart makes declarations portable.
diagramTitle: Connection and load divide reachability from target choice
diagramDesc: The connection reaches a directory, load selects result.csv, and rows are written there.
diagramFoot: A connection locates the system; load locates the object inside it.
diagramCaption: Reachability is shared context, not a writing policy.

label: load
title: load binds a target to a write policy
lead: Three executable CSV policies. The same writer can replace, append, or change batch size.
description: Name a destination target and define how final rows are loaded.
goalText: A target object, a mode, optional key columns, and a batch size.
cases:
destinations:
  output:
    type: csv
    connection: {base_path: out}
    load:
      table: result.csv
      mode: replace
      batch_size: 10000
the first batch replaces existing contents
later batches append within the same run
the verified job writes six rows

destinations:
  output:
    type: csv
    connection: {base_path: out}
    load:
      table: history.csv
      mode: append

destinations:
  output:
    type: csv
    connection: {base_path: out}
    load:
      table: result.csv
      mode: replace
      batch_size: 100
the target and mode remain unchanged
the requested write batch is smaller
tour: It belongs inside one destination declaration.
Use table for files and tables, or collection for MongoDB.
How this run changes the target.
Append is the default; replace clears first; upsert requires key columns and connector support.
Batch size is bounded; key is mandatory for an upsert declaration.
definition: load is the concrete write request passed to a destination connector.
It does not establish the connection or choose which destination the pipeline uses. It starts after pipeline.to and connector construction have resolved.
contains: Optional upsert keys and a batch size from 10 to 100,000.
thesisTitle: The mode describes this run
thesis: Connection tells Hydra where a writer can reach. load says what this particular run must do there, making append, replace, and upsert explicit at the edge.
diagramTitle: Load applies a policy to final rows
diagramDesc: Six final rows pass through replace mode and become the new contents of result.csv.
diagramFoot: The data is already final; load controls only its arrival.
diagramCaption: Target and policy travel together in one block.

label: steps
title: steps is the ordered execution plan
lead: Three valid lists. Add one operation at a time and keep the order visible.
description: Declare the ordered list of transformation operations.
goalText: One normalized operation after another, each receiving the previous result.
cases: one list entry becomes one operation

transformations:
  steps:
    - cast:
        mapping: {amount: float}
    - filter:
        expr: "amount > 50"

transformations:
  steps:
    - cast:
        mapping: {amount: float}
    - filter:
        expr: "amount > 50"
    - select:
        columns: [order_id, amount]
each entry has exactly one operation key
select receives only the filtered rows
tour: The list read by the transformation parser.
It may sit under transformations or directly at the file root.
An entry with several operation keys is not a step; the list makes boundaries explicit.
The block validated for that operation.
Each operation has its own model and required keys.
Top to bottom is runtime order.
The engine never reorders steps and each receives the previous output.
definition: steps is the ordered list of operations inside a job.
It is not a set of desired outcomes. Every list position is observable because the next operation receives the rows produced by the previous one.
contains: Each is a mapping with exactly one operation name.
The value is validated against that operation model.
Position is the execution order; no optimizer rearranges it.
thesisTitle: A step is one boundary
thesis: One list entry should answer one question: what operation runs next? The single-key shape makes the boundary visible and keeps ordering reviewable in plain YAML.
diagramTitle: Steps transform rows in list order
diagramDesc: Source rows pass through cast then filter, leaving six rows.
diagramFoot: Every arrow is a handoff from one list entry to the next.
diagramCaption: The list is the plan, and its order is the execution.

label: Columns
title: Column operations change the table contract
lead: Select, rename, and cast are three distinct moves. Each valid example changes one aspect only.
description: Select, rename and cast columns in a transformation plan.
goalText: Membership, names, or types — one dimension of the column contract at a time.
cases:
transformations:
  steps:
    - select:
        columns: [order_id, customer_id, amount, status]
the old name maps to the new name
values and row count stay unchanged
numeric expressions may now compare them
tour: One column operation in one step.
Select, rename, and cast have separate contracts.
The list also determines their output order.
Rename maps existing names to new names.
Later steps see only the new names.
Accepted types include int, float, str, bool, date, and datetime.
definition: Column operations are the three transformations that change which columns exist, what they are called, or what types they hold.
They do not filter rows or compute grouped results. Those effects belong to other operation families and should remain separate steps.
contains: Keeps an ordered, non-empty list of columns.
Maps old names to new names.
Maps columns to supported target types.
thesisTitle: Membership, names, and types are different
thesis: Keeping the three moves separate makes a pipeline readable. A reviewer can see whether a step narrows the table, changes its vocabulary, or converts its values.
diagramTitle: Column operations evolve a table contract
diagramDesc: Seven source columns are cast, renamed, and selected into a four-column output contract.
diagramFoot: Row membership is untouched; only the column contract changes.
diagramCaption: Each operation changes one dimension of the table.

label: Compute
title: Compute creates values without hiding the contract
lead: Calculate handles expressions; script handles declared custom outputs. Both name what they add.
description: Create derived columns with calculate or restricted script operations.
goalText: Named output columns derived from values already present in the current frame.
cases:
transformations:
  steps:
    - cast: {mapping: {amount: float}}
    - calculate:
        column: amount_with_tax
        expr: "amount * 1.2"
the expression uses the current frame

transformations:
  steps:
    - script:
        inputs: [quantity]
        outputs: {double_quantity: int}
        mode: row
        code: |
          double_quantity = quantity * 2
inputs and outputs form a contract
the code assigns the declared output

transformations:
  steps:
    - cast: {mapping: {amount: float}}
    - script:
        inputs: [amount]
        outputs: {amount_with_tax: float}
        mode: vectorized
        code: |
          amount_with_tax = amount * 1.2
the declared output is still required
tour: Calculate and script are separate because their contracts and execution models differ.
Values read from the current frame.
Calculate names them in an expression; script can declare an explicit input list.
The new columns are named before execution.
A script also declares each output type.
How a script evaluates its contract.
Row mode uses scalars; vectorized mode uses pandas Series in a restricted environment.
definition: Compute operations create new values from columns in the current transformation frame.
They do not reach external systems. calculate evaluates one pandas expression; script executes declared Python code in a restricted environment.
contains: One output column and one expression.
An optional list of columns made available to code.
A typed output mapping, execution mode, and required code block.
thesisTitle: Outputs are part of the declaration
thesis: Computation is easier to trust when every produced column is named up front. Calculate names one output; script declares an output mapping before any code runs.
diagramTitle: Compute maps current values to named outputs
diagramDesc: The amount column is multiplied by 1.2 and stored in amount_with_tax.
diagramFoot: The output name is visible in YAML before the expression executes.
diagramCaption: A computation is a contract from inputs to named outputs.

label: Aggregate
title: Aggregate changes the grain
lead: Three valid grouped summaries. The by list defines one output row per group.
description: Group rows and compute named aggregate outputs.
goalText: Thirty orders become one output row for each distinct status.
cases:
transformations:
  steps:
    - aggregate:
        by: [status]
        agg:
          total_amount: {func: sum, col: amount}
          order_count: {func: count, col: order_id}
each output names its source column and function

transformations:
  steps:
    - aggregate:
        by: [status]
        agg:
          amount: sum
the output keeps the source column name
the function is the mapping value
the same three groups are produced

transformations:
  steps:
    - aggregate:
        by: [status]
        agg:
          average_amount: {func: avg, col: amount}
group grain remains one row per status
tour: It consumes the current frame and returns a new frame at a different grain.
The non-empty list of grouping columns.
Every distinct combination becomes one output row.
A non-empty mapping of output columns.
Each entry chooses a function and, in long form, a source column.
The reducer applied inside each group.
Documented reducers include sum, count, mean/avg, min, max, first, and last.
definition: aggregate groups the current rows and computes named summary values at a new grain.
It is not a window calculation: source rows are replaced by one row per distinct by combination.
contains: Short form reuses a source name; long form separates output, function, and source column.
thesisTitle: The by list defines the grain
thesis: Read by before reading the functions. It tells you what one output row means; the aggregate mapping then tells you which facts are attached to that row.
diagramTitle: Aggregate changes row grain to group grain
diagramDesc: Thirty order rows are grouped by status into three summary rows.
diagramFoot: Grouping decides row identity; reducers decide the attached values.
diagramCaption: The output is a different table because its rows mean something different.

label: Combine
title: Combine brings in a second declared source
lead: Three valid union forms. Join, merge, and union all resolve right before the operation runs.
description: Combine the current frame with a second source using join, merge or union.
goalText: A second source is resolved and loaded before the transformation engine combines it.
cases:
transformations:
  steps:
    - union:
        right: src_orders_extra
        distinct: false
the right side is a declared source id
all four extra rows are appended

transformations:
  steps:
    - union:
        right: src_orders_extra
        distinct: true
the same right source is resolved

transformations:
  steps:
    - union:
        right:
          type: csv
          connection: {base_path: data/canonical}
          extract: {table: orders_extra.csv}
        distinct: false
right may be a complete inline source
the runner builds it before union
the operation still receives ready rows
tour: Join matches columns, merge reconciles by key, and union stacks rows.
Use a declared source identifier or a complete inline source declaration.
How join and merge align rows.
Join accepts a common key or separate left and right keys; merge requires a key.
How the two frames are reconciled.
Each operation exposes only the policy relevant to its semantics.
definition: Combine operations bring a second source into the current transformation frame.
The transformation engine does not open that source itself. The runner resolves right, loads its rows, and injects them before join, merge, or union executes.
contains: Matches rows with inner, left, right, or outer semantics.
Reconciles rows by a required key, optionally deleting unmatched left rows.
Stacks compatible rows and optionally removes duplicates.
thesisTitle: Right is prepared before the operation
thesis: A two-frame operation still has one transformation input. The runner turns right into ready rows first, so the engine receives two frames rather than a connector configuration.
diagramTitle: Combine adds a prepared right frame
diagramDesc: Thirty current rows are combined with four prepared right rows to produce 34 rows.
diagramFoot: The runner resolves right; the operation combines data frames.
diagramCaption: Connector work finishes before combination begins.

label: Reshape
title: Reshape changes where values live
lead: Unpivot, pivot, and transpose alter layout without inventing a second data source.
description: Change table layout with pivot, unpivot and transpose.
goalText: Rows become columns, columns become rows, or repeated value columns become observations.
cases:
transformations:
  steps:
    - unpivot:
        id_vars: [region]
        value_vars: [q1, q2, q3, q4]
        var_name: quarter
        value_name: revenue

transformations:
  steps:
    - pivot:
        index: [customer_id]
        column: status
        values: amount
        aggfunc: first

transformations:
  steps:
    - transpose:
        index_col: region
        header_name: metric
tour: Each operation changes axes in a different direction.
What remains stable while layout moves.
Read these keys first to understand the output row identity.
Which cells move into the new layout.
Unpivot gathers columns; pivot distributes one values column.
Explicit names keep the reshaped table readable downstream.
definition: Reshape operations change the arrangement of values across rows and columns.
They do not join another source or summarize groups by themselves. Pivot may aggregate collisions, but its primary responsibility is layout.
contains: Turns values from one column into output columns.
Turns several value columns into repeated rows.
Exchanges the row and column axes.
thesisTitle: Name the identity before moving values
thesis: A reshape is understandable when the stable identity is explicit. Read index, id_vars, or index_col first; then follow the values that move around it.
diagramTitle: Unpivot turns repeated columns into observations
diagramDesc: Five regional rows with four quarter columns become twenty region-quarter observations.
diagramFoot: The same values remain; their coordinates change.
diagramCaption: Reshape changes layout, not the source of the values.

label: name and version
title: A workflow needs an identity before it runs
lead: Three complete identities. Name labels the run; version records the manifest shape.
description: Name a workflow and record the manifest version it targets.
goalText: A required run name, an optional description, and a version defaulting to 1.0.
cases:
workflow:
  version: "1.0"
  name: docs_workflow
  description: Two actions used by the docs.
  steps:
    - {name: note, type: action, action: log, params: {message: "Ready."}}
version is stored with the definition
description explains intent without changing execution

workflow:
  name: docs_workflow
  steps:
    - {name: note, type: action, action: log, params: {message: "Ready."}}
one required name labels the workflow
tour: The root mapping for one orchestration graph.
Identity, trigger, and steps all live below this key.
It appears in runner logs and the WorkflowResult object.
It defaults to 1.0 and is stored; no alternate workflow grammar is selected today.
It explains the purpose of the graph and does not affect scheduling.
definition: Workflow name is the required identity used in logs and results; version records the manifest shape the definition targets.
Neither field establishes dependencies. The graph comes from steps; identity makes that graph recognizable to people and tools.
contains: A string carried into workflow results.
Description documents purpose without changing the run.
thesisTitle: Identity labels the graph; it does not build it
thesis: Choose a stable name that survives individual run IDs. Keep version as manifest context, then let trigger and steps carry the operational meaning.
diagramTitle: Workflow identity travels into results
diagramDesc: The docs_workflow name from workflow.yaml labels the resulting workflow run.
diagramFoot: Steps may change over time; the workflow name keeps the graph recognizable.
diagramCaption: Identity follows the graph from declaration to result.

label: trigger
title: trigger declares how a workflow may start
lead: Manual, schedule, and webhook are three valid entry policies. The graph below them stays the same.
description: Declare whether a workflow starts manually, on a schedule or through a webhook.
goalText: The intended entry point for the graph, separate from its dependency structure.
cases: manual is the default trigger type
the CLI can start the graph directly

workflow:
  name: daily_notes
  trigger:
    type: schedule
    cron: "0 6 * * *"
  steps:
    - {name: note, type: action, action: log, params: {message: "Ready."}}
webhook is an accepted trigger type
the manifest describes entry, not HTTP deployment
tour: The entry policy attached to the workflow.
It defaults to a manual trigger when the block is omitted.
One of manual, schedule, or webhook.
The value is validated by the workflow model before execution.
It is required only when trigger type is schedule.
The same dependency graph can be started through different entry policies.
definition: trigger declares the intended entry policy for a workflow graph: manual, schedule, or webhook.
It is not the scheduler or HTTP endpoint itself. Those platform concerns live outside the DSL; this block records the contract the platform should use.
contains: Manual by default, or schedule/webhook when declared.
Dependencies and failure policies remain on steps.
thesisTitle: Entry policy is not execution order
thesis: Trigger answers when or how the graph becomes eligible to start. Once started, depends_on still decides which nodes can run.
diagramTitle: Trigger feeds one unchanged workflow graph
diagramDesc: Manual, scheduled, or webhook entry passes through trigger into the same dependency graph.
diagramFoot: Changing the entry policy does not rewrite the graph.
diagramCaption: One graph can have one declared way in.

label: steps
title: Workflow steps are nodes, not a sequence
lead: Job nodes, action nodes, and dependent nodes. The edges decide order and parallelism.
description: Declare job and action nodes in a workflow dependency graph.
goalText: Named nodes grouped by dependency readiness, with independent nodes allowed to run together.
cases:
workflow:
  name: one_note
  steps:
    - name: note
      type: action
      action: log
      params: {message: "Ready."}
action selects a built-in side effect
one node forms one execution group

workflow:
  name: one_job
  steps:
    - name: load_orders
      type: job
      job: ../../minimal_csv
job points to a Hydra job directory
the node delegates row processing to that job
one node forms one execution group

workflow:
  name: two_notes
  steps:
    - {name: prepare, type: action, action: log, params: {message: "Ready."}}
    - name: publish
      type: action
      action: log
      params: {message: "Published."}
      depends_on: [prepare]
publish names prepare as a dependency
the runner builds two sequential groups
tour: The node list for one workflow.
Unlike transformation steps, vertical position alone does not establish runtime order.
A unique name inside the graph.
Job or action, with its matching target.
A job needs a job path; an action needs an action name.
The incoming edges of this node.
Every listed predecessor must complete before the node becomes ready.
definition: Workflow steps is the list of named nodes in an orchestration graph.
It is not an ordered transformation list. Runtime groups come from depends_on; independent nodes may run in parallel even when written on different lines.
contains: A job directory or action name with parameters.
Dependencies, condition, enabled flag, failure policy, and optional retry.
thesisTitle: Edges make the schedule
thesis: List order keeps YAML readable. Dependency edges create the executable plan, so review depends_on whenever you need to understand sequencing or parallelism.
diagramTitle: Dependencies turn workflow steps into a graph
diagramDesc: The publish step depends on prepare and therefore runs in the next execution group.
diagramFoot: Without the edge, both actions would be ready together.
diagramCaption: Names create nodes; depends_on creates order.

label: retry
title: retry wraps one step in an attempt policy
lead: No retry, fixed delay, and exponential backoff are all valid. Success stops the loop immediately.
description: Configure retry count, delay and backoff for one workflow step.
goalText: One step execution, repeated only after failure and only up to the declared maximum.
cases:
workflow:
  name: notes
  steps:
    - {name: note, type: action, action: log, params: {message: "Ready."}}
the first success completes the node

workflow:
  name: notes
  steps:
    - name: note
      type: action
      action: log
      params: {message: "Ready."}
      retry: {max: 2, delay: 1, backoff: fixed}
max counts re-attempts after the first failure
success ends the loop before retries are used

workflow:
  name: notes
  steps:
    - name: note
      type: action
      action: log
      params: {message: "Ready."}
      retry: {max: 3, delay: 2, backoff: exponential}
the first retry waits two seconds
later waits double from the base delay
at most four total attempts occur
tour: The attempt policy attached to one step.
Different steps may carry different policies.
A max of two permits three total attempts.
Zero is allowed and performs immediate re-attempts.
Exponential multiplies the base delay by powers of two.
definition: retry is the re-attempt policy around one workflow step.
It is not a workflow-wide restart. Completed predecessor nodes stay complete, and the policy only repeats the step that failed.
contains: Number of retries after the initial attempt; default zero.
Base wait in seconds; default zero.
thesisTitle: Max counts retries, not attempts
thesis: A policy with max: 2 allows the initial attempt plus two re-attempts. Reading max this way prevents an off-by-one expectation during incident review.
diagramTitle: Retry adds attempts around one workflow step
diagramDesc: One initial attempt may be followed by up to two retries, stopping as soon as the step succeeds.
diagramFoot: The wrapper repeats one node, not the whole workflow.
diagramCaption: Retries are local and success short-circuits the policy.

label: filter.expr
title: filter.expr decides which rows continue
lead: Three valid pandas-query expressions. Each returns a boolean decision for every current row.
description: Write boolean row predicates for the filter operation.
goalText: A true or false decision per row, evaluated against columns in the current frame.
cases: the expression compares one current column
string literals are quoted inside the expression
status is read from the current frame
both names must exist when this step runs
tour: It preserves columns and removes rows whose predicate is false.
Hydra passes it to pandas query using the Python expression engine.
Names resolve in the current frame.
Earlier cast, rename, and select steps determine which names and types exist here.
Use explicit parentheses when a longer expression mixes boolean operators.
definition: filter.expr is a boolean expression evaluated once across the current table to decide which rows continue.
It is not validated against runtime column types by hdrctl validate. Earlier steps must prepare both names and types before the filter runs.
contains: Resolved by pandas query at this step.
Numbers, quoted strings, and comparison operators.
thesisTitle: The expression sees the current frame
thesis: A filter never reaches back to source columns. Rename or cast first, and the expression sees only those resulting names and values.
diagramTitle: Filter expression turns rows into boolean decisions
diagramDesc: Thirty current rows are evaluated against amount greater than 50 and six true rows continue.
diagramFoot: False rows stop here; every column on true rows continues.
diagramCaption: A filter changes membership, not the column contract.

label: calculate.expr
title: calculate.expr produces one named column
lead: Three valid pandas-eval expressions. The output name and the formula stay separate.
description: Write an expression that derives one output column from the current frame.
goalText: One new or replaced column, with one value for every current row.
cases:
transformations:
  steps:
    - cast: {mapping: {amount: float}}
    - calculate:
        column: amount_with_tax
        expr: "amount * 1.2"

transformations:
  steps:
    - cast: {mapping: {amount: float, quantity: int}}
    - calculate:
        column: line_weight
        expr: "amount * quantity"
two current columns feed the expression

transformations:
  steps:
    - cast: {mapping: {amount: float}}
    - calculate:
        column: amount
        expr: "amount * 1.2"
an existing column name may be the output
the expression reads its pre-step values
later steps see only the replacement
tour: Each calculate step has one output name and one expression.
A new name adds a column; an existing name replaces it.
It is evaluated against columns in the current transformation frame.
Types must be ready before evaluation.
Validation checks manifest shape, not the runtime compatibility of the formula.
definition: calculate.expr is the formula used to produce one named output column from the current frame.
It does not filter rows and it cannot declare several outputs at once. Use separate calculate steps or a script with an explicit output mapping.
contains: Names available when the step begins.
Evaluated by pandas eval with the Python engine.
thesisTitle: Name the output outside the formula
thesis: Separating column from expr makes assignment explicit. A reader can identify what changes without parsing the expression text.
diagramTitle: Calculate expression maps current columns to one output
diagramDesc: The current amount value is multiplied by 1.2 and assigned to amount_with_tax.
diagramFoot: Every current row remains; each receives one calculated value.
diagramCaption: The formula computes; column names the destination.

label: step.when
title: step.when gates one workflow node
lead: Three safe boolean guards. A true guard runs the node; a false guard skips it and its dependants.
description: Conditionally run a workflow step with a safe boolean expression.
goalText: Whether one ready node may execute after its dependencies have completed.
cases:
workflow:
  name: guarded_note
  steps:
    - name: note
      type: action
      action: log
      params: {message: "Ready."}
      when: "1 == 1"
the expression is parsed as a safe AST

workflow:
  name: guarded_note
  steps:
    - name: note
      type: action
      action: log
      params: {message: "Ready."}
      when: "'prod' in ['dev', 'prod']"
no arbitrary function call is available

workflow:
  name: guarded_note
  steps:
    - name: note
      type: action
      action: log
      params: {message: "Ready."}
      when: "{{ env:HYDRA_ENV }} == 'prod'"
the placeholder is resolved before comparison
numeric-looking values are coerced when both sides are numeric
the AST still contains only allowed nodes
tour: Dependencies are checked before its when expression.
Empty or omitted means the ready step runs normally.
Arbitrary variable names, calls, attributes, and indexing are not allowed.
A skipped node also prevents dependent nodes from becoming runnable.
definition: step.when is a safe boolean guard evaluated after dependencies are complete and before one workflow node runs.
It is not Python eval. Hydra parses an allow-listed AST of comparisons, boolean operators, literals, lists, tuples, and parameter/environment placeholders.
contains: Equality and ordered comparisons, with numeric coercion when appropriate.
Literals plus {{ param:NAME }} and {{ env:NAME }} placeholders.
thesisTitle: Ready does not always mean run
thesis: Dependencies decide when a node is ready. when makes the final admission decision for that node without changing the topology of the graph.
diagramTitle: When gates a ready workflow step
diagramDesc: After dependencies complete, a true when expression admits the step to execution.
diagramFoot: A false guard records a skip instead of running the node.
diagramCaption: Dependency readiness and conditional admission are separate decisions.

label: script.code
title: script.code runs inside a declared boundary
lead: Row and vectorized scripts stay explicit about inputs, outputs, types, and mode.
description: Write restricted Python code inside a script transformation contract.
goalText: Only declared inputs, approved builtins, and assignments to declared outputs.
cases:
transformations:
  steps:
    - script:
        inputs: [amount]
        outputs: {amount_with_tax: float}
        mode: row
        code: |
          amount_with_tax = amount * 1.2
amount is a scalar for each row
the code assigns one declared output

transformations:
  steps:
    - script:
        inputs: [amount]
        outputs: {amount_with_tax: float}
        mode: vectorized
        code: |
          amount_with_tax = amount * 1.2
one expression handles the whole column

transformations:
  steps:
    - script:
        inputs: [amount]
        outputs:
          amount_with_tax: float
          doubled: float
        mode: row
        code: |
          amount_with_tax = amount * 1.2
          doubled = amount * 2
both outputs are declared with types
both are assigned by the code
tour: Its contract surrounds the code block.
Duplicates are removed and names are normalized before execution.
Allowed types include int, float, str, bool, date, datetime, and any.
How values are exposed and what is executed.
Row uses scalars; vectorized uses Series; the runtime restricts imports and builtins.
definition: script.code is restricted Python executed inside an explicit input/output contract.
It is not an escape to the host Python process. Imports are unavailable, builtins are allow-listed, and outputs must be declared before code runs.
contains: Code that derives declared output variables.
Common numeric, collection, iteration, formatting, and type helpers.
Inputs are declared columns; outputs are declared names and types.
thesisTitle: The contract is larger than the code
thesis: Read inputs, outputs, and mode before reading the code block. They define what the script may consume, must produce, and how values appear during execution.
diagramTitle: Script code is enclosed by an input-output contract
diagramDesc: The amount input enters restricted code and produces declared typed output columns.
diagramFoot: The code cannot widen its own contract after execution starts.
diagramCaption: Custom logic remains reviewable because its boundary is YAML.

label: {{ param }} and {{ env }}
title: Parameters and environment are substituted before parsing
lead: Full-value and embedded placeholders are both valid. Full values preserve their resolved type.
description: Substitute job parameters and environment variables into YAML before model validation.
goalText: Resolved values, with types preserved when a placeholder occupies the whole YAML value.
cases: the parameter is resolved before transform parsing

sources:
  input:
    type: csv
    extract:
      table: orders.csv
      batch_size: "{{ param:BATCH_SIZE }}"
the whole YAML value is one placeholder
an integer parameter remains an integer
the source model receives a typed batch size
the OS environment supplies the value
MIN_AMOUNT=50 yields the same six rows
tour: A value resolved before Pydantic models see YAML.
Parameter names and environment names use the same placeholder grammar.
Parameters follow Hydra's layered precedence; env reads the process environment.
A placeholder occupying the whole value preserves type.
An integer can therefore reach an integer model field without string coercion.
A placeholder inside larger text becomes a string substitution.
This is how numeric thresholds become part of filter expressions.
definition: {{ param:NAME }} and {{ env:NAME }} are placeholders resolved before the YAML structure is validated by DSL models.
They are not runtime expression variables. After substitution, operations receive ordinary strings, numbers, booleans, lists, or mappings.
contains: Resolved from declarations and layered values, with CLI overrides strongest.
Read from the current process environment.
A full placeholder preserves type; an embedded placeholder produces text.
thesisTitle: Whole values keep their type
thesis: Use a placeholder as the entire YAML value when the receiving key expects an integer, boolean, list, or mapping. Embed it in text only when text is the intended result.
diagramTitle: Interpolation resolves values before DSL parsing
diagramDesc: The MIN_AMOUNT parameter is substituted into expression text before the transformation model parses it.
diagramFoot: The parser never receives placeholder syntax; it receives the resolved value.
diagramCaption: Interpolation prepares the manifest; the DSL then validates the result.
